item.title: Permafrost carbon–climate feedback amplifies Earth system tipping risks
item.dc:creator: Norman Julius Steinert, Gregory Munday, Marit Sandstad, Benjamin Mark Sanderson, Nico Wunderling
item.description:
Environmental Research Letters — matched: ice sheet, Antarctic, Greenland, West Antarctic, tipping point, tipping element, overshoot, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, overturning circulation, permafrost, Earth system, climate feedback, climate change, global warming
Abstract Global warming leads to widespread permafrost thaw and subsequent emissions of carbon dioxide and methane, driving the permafrost carbon–climate feedback (PCF) which amplifies climate change. Many current-generation climate models omit this feedback, limiting projections of long-term temperature outcomes and associated Earth system tipping risks. Here, we investigate how this feedback affects the risk and timing of crossing tipping points in the Earth system by integrating permafrost carbon emissions into temperature projections for idealized stabilization and overshoot scenarios. In a conceptual network model of interacting climate tipping elements—including the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, and the Amazon rainforest, we find that PCF leads to additional warming that increases the probability of exceeding one or more tipping elements by up to 50% and can substantially accelerate the timing of tipping events by hundreds of years. The effect of PCF on tipping risk and acceleration is particularly evident in overshoot scenarios with lower peak temperatures below 2–3 ∘ C or peak cumulative emissions of below 2000 PgC. Considering PCF, therefore, narrows the critical temperature space for overshoot pathways. Our results highlight that failing to account for PCF underestimates both climate risks and the urgency of mitigation, increasing the likelihood of tipping events across the Earth system.

item.title: Early warning of critical transitions: Distinguishing tipping points from turing destabilizations
item.dc:creator: Paul A. Sanders, Robbin Bastiaansen
item.description:
Physica D Nonlinear Phenomena — matched: tipping point, bifurcation
Current early warning signs for tipping points often fail to distinguish between catastrophic shifts and less dramatic state changes, such as spatial pattern formation. This paper introduces a novel method that addresses this limitation by providing more information about the type of bifurcation being approached starting from a spatially homogeneous system state. This method relies on estimates of the dispersion relation from noisy spatio-temporal data, which reveals whether the system is approaching a spatially homogeneous (tipping) or spatially heterogeneous (Turing patterning) bifurcation. Using a modified Klausmeier model, we validate this method on synthetic data, exploring its performance under varying conditions including noise properties and distance to bifurcation. We also determine the data requirements for optimal performance. Our results indicate the promise of a new spatial early warning system built on this method to improve predictions of future transitions in many climate subsystems and ecosystems, which is critical for effective conservation and management in a rapidly changing world.

item.title: Review Article: A Systematic Review of Acquisition and Processing Approaches for Earth Observations of Arctic Sea Ice Melt Ponds
item.dc:creator: Sara Aparício, Simon Driscoll, Daniela Flocco
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Arctic, sea ice
This review article explains how scientists monitor Arctic melt ponds, which are pools of water that form on sea ice in late spring and early summer. These ponds absorb more sunlight than ice, speeding up melting and reinforcing warming. We examine satellite and field measurements, compare the strengths and limits of different tools, and review available datasets. The study highlights current knowledge gaps and identifies priorities to improve future observations and climate predictions.

item.title: Improved CMIP6 projections of Hudson Bay region navigability using bias correction and route continuity
item.dc:creator: Armina Soleymani, Alex Crawford, Lawrence Mudryk, Feiyue Wang
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: sea ice, CMIP, global warming
Hudson Bay’s seasonal sea ice limits maritime access to the Port of Churchill, and although we know future warming will lengthen the navigable period, how quickly it will lengthen is unclear. Based on several methods for making future projections, the navigable period for the route from Churchill to the Labrador Sea has lengthened by about 4 weeks since the 1980s. In the future, it is projected to lengthen by about 2 weeks for each additional 0.5 °C of global warming.

item.title: To tip or not to tip
item.dc:creator: Reyk Börner, Henk A. Dijkstra
item.description:
Earth System Dynamics — matched: tipping point
Tipping points have become a popular concept in earth sciences and for communicating climate risk. However, we identify three issues with existing tipping definitions that cause confusion about what "tipping" means. We propose to define a tipping event as a persistent nonlinear transition, shifting focus from abruptness and irreversibility to nonlinear response and self-amplifying feedback. We illustrate how our definition can be applied in practice to determine whether tipping occurs or not.

item.title: ChinaMet: A multisource integrated high-resolution multi-variable meteorological dataset for China
item.dc:creator: Yingyi Hu, Ling Zhang, Yanbo Zhao, Tao Che
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: reanalysis, downscaling
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) ChinaMet is a high-resolution meteorological dataset for China covering 1980–2024. It integrates over 2,300 station observations with satellite, reanalysis, and auxiliary data through a merging–downscaling framework, providing eight variables at 0.01° resolution. ChinaMet offers continuous and spatially detailed meteorological forcing for hydrological, ecological, agricultural, and climate applications.

item.title: SWORD-CTRIP mapping (SCM v1.0): a confidence-aware framework for mapping satellite-derived river reaches to gridded routing networks
item.dc:creator: Kaushlendra Verma, Simon Munier
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: data assimilation
Satellite provide river observations as vector reaches, while large-scale hydrological models represent rivers on gridded routing networks. This structural mismatch limits direct data assimilation. We present a global, confidence-aware framework that assigns vector river reaches to routing pixels using geometric and hydrological consistency criteria. Results show that most routing pixels can be assigned with high confidence while preserving basin-scale drainage topology into hydrological models.

item.title: Linking ridge shapes to the ice thickness distribution via discrete element simulations
item.dc:creator: Marek Muchow, Einar Ólason, Arttu Polojärvi
item.description:
The Cryosphere
Sea-ice ridges increase the ice thickness beyond values created by thermodynamic growth as they consist of broken ice pieces piled together. We simulated ridging using a discrete-element-method model, in which the ice is described by individual ice blocks, which can break apart and form ridges. We observe both triangular and trapezoidal ridges. Both ridge shapes influence the amount of thick ice after deformation, which we describe with an analytical function.

item.title: Development of ACFIRE version 1.0: a mesoscale model with forest canopy and fire behavior submodels
item.dc:creator: Michael T. Kiefer, Shiyuan Zhong, Joseph J. Charney, Xindi Bian, Warren E. Heilman, Joseph Seitz, … (+7)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
We introduce a modeling system that couples a surface fire model with a canopy-resolving atmospheric model to simulate two-way fire–atmosphere interactions. Using data from a New Jersey Pine Barrens prescribed burn, we show that the system reproduces observed fire-perturbed atmospheric variables and surface fire spread. Our results demonstrate the potential of dynamic coupling to improve surface fire behavior prediction in complex forests and enable future integration of crown-fire processes.
